problem.claim: The paper examines how to evaluate and improve visibility into AI agents’ decision-making, especially through chain-of-thought monitoring.

gap.claim: It identifies monitorability as potentially fragile across training procedures, data sources, and continued system scaling.

contributions.claim: Proposes three evaluation archetypes, a new monitorability metric, and a broad evaluation suite.
Studies how pre-training model size, inference-time compute, reasoning effort, and monitor compute relate to monitorability.
Investigates improving monitorability through monitor access to chain of thought and follow-up questions with follow-up chain of thought.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present the three evaluation archetypes, monitorability metric, and evaluation suite as new components of their proposed evaluation approach.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that chain-of-thought monitoring outperforms action-only monitoring in practical settings, while frontier models are generally but not perfectly monitorable.

The authors report that longer chain-of-thoughts are typically more monitorable; at fixed capability, a smaller model with higher reasoning effort can provide higher monitorability at greater inference-compute cost.

The authors report that increasing a weak monitor’s test-time compute, giving it access to the agent’s chain of thought, and using follow-up questions with follow-up chain of thought can improve monitorability.

narrative_sequence.summary: Safe deployment may require visibility into agent decisions, but chain-of-thought monitorability may be fragile under changing training, data, and scaling conditions.
The paper introduces three evaluation archetypes, a monitorability metric, and a broad evaluation suite.
The authors report advantages over action-only monitoring, generally non-perfect monitorability, and relationships between reasoning length, model size, capability, and compute.
The authors report gains from additional monitor compute, chain-of-thought access, and follow-up questioning with follow-up chain of thought.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs an evaluation taxonomy and metric with analyses of scaling and concrete interventions such as monitor compute, chain-of-thought access, and follow-up questions.

lessons.interpretation: A monitoring paper can make its central property more actionable by connecting measurement design to controllable improvement levers and explicit resource tradeoffs.
lessons.application: When studying a new oversight property, define evaluation archetypes and a metric, then test both scaling relationships and interventions that may improve the property.
lessons.exception: This structure may be unsuitable when the property cannot be operationalized reliably or when interventions alter the target behavior being measured.

unknowns: The abstract does not define the monitorability metric, evaluation tasks, model populations, or what constitutes a practical setting.
The reported comparisons and scaling trends lack quantitative effect sizes, uncertainty, and detailed experimental conditions.
It is unclear whether follow-up questions improve monitorability at additional capability, latency, or inference-compute costs.
